# Research sources

The implementation is a perceptual synthesizer, not a ballistic simulator. These sources guided the shape and timing of the acoustic layers.

1. Robert C. Maher, **Summary of Gun Shot Acoustics** (Montana State University, 2006). Describes the Mach cone, rapid positive overpressure, negative-pressure ramp, abrupt offset and typical sub-200 microsecond N-wave interval.
   - https://www.montana.edu/rmaher/publications/maher_aac_0406.pdf
2. Robert C. Maher, **Modeling and Signal Processing of Acoustic Gunshot Recordings** (IEEE DSP Workshop, 2006). Describes bullet shock-wave geometry, ground reflections and the effect of downrange deceleration.
   - https://www.montana.edu/rmaher/publications/maher_ieeedsp_0906_257-261.pdf
3. Roland Stoughton, **Measurements of small-caliber ballistic shock waves in air**, Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 102, 781-787 (1997). Reports measured waveform shape, period, amplitude, distance scaling and turbulence-related rise-time variation.
   - https://doi.org/10.1121/1.419904
4. Gregory A. Flamme and William J. Murphy, **Auditory risk of exposure to ballistic N-waves from bullets**, International Journal of Audiology 58:sup1, S58-S64 (2019). Confirms the high impulsive level and importance of distance from the trajectory.
   - https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/217132/cdc_217132_DS1.pdf
5. NASA, **Like the Sound of Thunder**. Concise explanation that a supersonic bullet crack is a miniature sonic boom generated by a shock wave.
   - https://www.nasa.gov/image-article/like-sound-of-thunder-2/
